summary:
Beyond the seat tables, the 2026 polls carry four kinds of information the forecast uses or could use: how firm each list's support is, how large the undecided pool is and which way it leans, how voters move between lists, and which governments voters will accept. Since the 15 Oct desks, the Central Elections Committee posted six filings the model has not parsed (refs 4202-4212). They hold the campaign's best non-seat data.

Certainty. Lazar/Walla (12 Oct, n=601, CEC 4207) published the first per-list table. 45% of decided voters are completely certain: coalition voters 54%, opposition voters 35%. The firmest lists are the Joint List (81%), Likud (68%) and RZP-Zehut (62%). Together is the softest (23%), followed by the Reservists (28%), Ra'am and UTJ (35%), Otzma (38%), the Democrats (39%), Yashar (40%) and YB (41%). Rescaled to the certainty layer's mean, Together and Yashar match the model's values. YB, Otzma and the declared UTJ tier come out too firm; Likud, RZP and the Joint List too soft. Channel 13's sector samples (13 Oct, CEC 4210) put haredi (65.5% very sure) and Arab (79.5%) choice certainty far above Jewish adults (46.4%). That argues for shrinking Lazar's small-n UTJ figure toward a high haredi tier. JPPI's August wave confirms the centre is softest (completely decided: left 81, centre 41, right 64).

Undecideds. Definitions vary from 1.3% (Channel 14) to 30% (Kan). Comparable lines have been falling: Lazar from 13% (16 Sept) to 5.2% (15 Oct), Midgam 8.1%, Channel 13 11.7% of Jewish adults. Channel 13 asked its 70 undecided Jewish adults which way they lean: 30% change bloc, 19% Netanyahu bloc, 6% unaligned, 40% no lean. That is a 61.5/38.5 split of the bloc-leaned, against 52/48 among decided voters. N12's 12 Oct breakdown has only 0.2% of the electorate torn between blocs. Both imply the model's undecided transfer is about twice what the October data support. It moves about 0.7 seats per side and rests on a 0.71 leaned fraction from a single July N12 item.

Turnout. Every house that asks finds opposition voters more certain to vote than coalition voters (N12 81-82 vs 75; Lazar 86 vs 81; Kan 'considering not voting' 16 vs 23). Self-reports are badly inflated, though: in IDI's August 2022 index only 3% of Jews and 26% of Arabs said they would not vote, and 81% of Channel 13's 2026 Arab phone sample say they will certainly vote. Validation studies (Rogers and Aida; Pew) show self-prediction is a weak screen. Any bloc-turnout term should therefore enter only as a shrunk differential.

Flows and second choices. N12 (9 Sept) shows Amcha drawing 48% from the 2022 RZP-Otzma list and 44% from Likud, and Yashar drawing 38% from Yesh Atid, 24% from National Unity and 16% from Likud. Channel 13 finds 28% of Likud supporters considering Otzma and 52% of Democrats considering Yashar. Coalition voters care much more that their bloc leader heads the largest list (Channel 14: 73% vs 40% very important). This supports the gevalt coupling and points to a Yashar consolidation term in the change bloc. JPPI shows recall-based items are distorted, so survey flows should not displace the kalpi transition matrix.

Leaders and coalitions. Eisenkot leads Netanyahu head-to-head in each house's latest poll except Channel 14's (Midgam 45-35, Lazar 48-41, Kan 43-38). Netanyahu leads multi-candidate questions because the alternatives split. Named-leader unity governments are rejected by the other side's voters (61-17, 79-8), while 87% of change-bloc voters accept some form of Arab-party reliance (Kantar).

Missing seat polls: Direct Polls/i24 13 Oct (n=1,210), Channel 14/Next Data 14 Oct (n=568) and Kantar/Israel Hayom 14-15 Oct (n=551).

findings.claim: The first per-list certainty table of the campaign (Lazar for Walla, 12 Oct) shows choice certainty differs sharply by list and by bloc: coalition voters are far firmer than opposition voters, Together is the softest list, and the Joint List and Likud are the firmest. The standard error is therefore 5-10 points per list. findings.claim: Channel 13's 13 Oct filing contains a new undecided-lean measurement. Of 70 undecided Jewish adults, under half lean toward a bloc-aligned list, and those who do split about 61/39 for the change bloc. The lean is a much weaker anti-Netanyahu tilt than the July N12 measurement the model pools. Haredi and Arab undecideds lean to their own lists.

findings.model_link: Undecided-lean layer: U_LEANED_FRAC 0.71 and U_LEAN_BASE 0.775, from N12 30 Jul (55/16/29, about 60 undecideds); data/undecided_leans.csv has only that row. In the model's own formula (bayes_model l.1398-1403) the per-side transfer is leaned fraction x (lean - 0.52). For this wave that is 0.488 x (0.615 - 0.52) = 0.046 of the pool. The shipped layer gives 0.71 x (0.647 - 0.52) = 0.090 at today's posterior lean, which is the site's ~0.7 seats per side, and 0.181 at the N12 base lean. This wave alone therefore supports about half the shipped transfer. Adding this row (n_undecided 70, anti 0.300, nb 0.188, none 0.512) moves the pooled Beta mean only from 0.647 to 0.638. The larger correction is to the hard-coded leaned fraction: n-weighted over the two waves it is 0.59, not 0.71.

findings.model_link: Undecided pool and cross-bloc transfer (U_POOL, CHURN_SPLIT). With only 0.2% torn across blocs, any bloc-level effect of the undecided must come from the composition of within-bloc waverers. Here that is 2.6 opposition vs 1.8 NB, 59% opposition against about 52% of the decided bloc vote. If a house allocated these waverers proportionally, the opposition would be under-credited by about 0.3% of the electorate per side (about 0.4 seats) before any turnout haircut. Midgam's own 'cracking' of waverers (footnote to CEC 4202) probably already assigns them within their bloc, so the true residual is smaller. Corroborates DYN-F14 (9 Oct Ulpan Shishi: 5.4% of the undecided between blocs).
findings.site_use: most of today's undecideds are choosing within a bloc

findings.claim: A third of voters say they will decide in the final days, on election day or in the booth, about the share who say they decided that late in 2022. Late decision is common, but its size is stable across cycles.

findings.claim: Two polls show a large 'vote for the bloc's largest list' reservoir that is asymmetric by bloc. Coalition voters care far more that their bloc leader's party is the largest. A strategist's poll puts the potential consolidation at 18 seats if Likud and Yashar run neck and neck.
findings.quant: Channel 14 / Next Data, 12 Oct 2026 (CEC 4209; n=538 of 12,794 invited, 5% response, MoE +-4.4), weighted, split by 2022 vote. 'How important is it that the party of the bloc's lead candidate is also the largest in the Knesset?' Very important: coalition-2022 voters 73.3%, opposition-2022 voters 40.4%; important 17.7/31.6; not really 7.0/18.5; not at all 2.0/9.4. Same filing: 95.2% say they have already decided (undecided line 1.3%); 9.4% say the Mandelblit testimony will change their vote (11.6% of coalition-2022 voters, 6.8% of opposition-2022 voters). Israel Hayom column by campaign strategist Moshe Klughaft, 15 Oct 2026, reporting 'a special study we did this week' (pollster, n and wording of sampling not stated). 'If the polls show Likud and Yashar close, is it important to vote for the largest party in the bloc?': about 8 seats shared by Bennett and Liberman could move to Eisenkot, and about 3 of Golan's and 3 of Ben-Gvir's to Netanyahu, 18 seats in total. Same study: 'if there is no decision', repeat elections 67% vs unity with rotation 33%. Rotation support by party: Winter voters 64%, Hendel-Zelekha 50%, Liberman 42%, Bennett 36%; NB parties, Yashar and the Democrats below average.

findings.claim: Voters want their own camp to govern. When neither bloc wins, preferences between a unity government and repeat elections depend heavily on wording: unity wins when the leader is unnamed, and repeat elections or rejection win when rotation or the other side's leader is spelled out.
findings.quant: Lazar/Maariv 14-15 Oct (n=700): if there is no decision, unity government 55%, another election 27%, DK 18%. 54% of opposition voters would accept unity only if a change-bloc figure leads it; among coalition voters 36% prefer a Netanyahu-led unity government vs 32% another election. Optimistic their bloc will win: 79% (coalition 90%, opposition 75%). Kantar/Israel Hayom (7-8 Oct, n=555): if no bloc reaches a majority, about a third in each bloc prefer unity, while 54% of coalition voters and 47% of opposition voters prefer repeat elections (Together voters the exception); 75% of coalition voters and 78% of opposition voters fear for the country if the other bloc governs. Klughaft study (PBV-F12): repeat elections 67% vs rotation unity 33%. JPPI October 2026 (618 Jewish + 203 Arab): 'form a government including both Likud and the largest party in the change bloc' want 27, do not want 60, DK 14 (do not want: left 87, centre-left 80, centre 74, right 54; centre-right 41 for / 48 against). JPPI July 2026: right-led coalition 30%, change-led 35%, broad cross-bloc 28%. Channel 13, 24 Sept: broad unity 31, full right 29, full opposition 25.

More than 130,000 ex-USSR-born voters aged 18+ have arrived since 2022 (over 255,000 since 2014).

findings.claim: Israeli surveys sharply under-report abstention. In August 2022 only 3% of Jewish and 26% of Arab respondents said they did not intend to vote, against national turnout of 70.6% and Arab turnout of 53.2% that November. Self-reported turnout intention cannot be used at face value.
findings.quant: IDI Israeli Voice Index, August 2022 (fieldwork 21-24 Aug 2022 by Midgam; internet and phone; 602 Hebrew and 152 Arabic interviews; MoE +-3.59%). Q5, 'At the upcoming Knesset elections, who do you intend to vote for?': 'Don't intend to vote' Jews 3.0%, Arabs 25.9% (Arabs also 30.3% 'don't know who they vote for'). Q4: 'Don't intend to vote' general public 3.8% (Jews 1.8, Arabs 13.8). Official 1 Nov 2022 turnout: 70.6% national; Arab and Druze localities 53.2% (Bayan 28, SEC-F01). The gap between stated non-intention and actual abstention is about 21 points for Arabs (25.9 vs 46.8) and over 20 points nationally (3.8 vs 29.4). Part of the gap may be the denominator: the official roll includes citizens living abroad, which is not sourced in this desk. In 2026, Channel 13's Arab phone sample says 81.1% 'will certainly vote' (PBV-F21), Lazar's national sample 78% (PBV-F07).

findings.claim: Validation studies find that self-predicted turnout is a weak, biased screen. Many self-predicted voters do not vote and many self-predicted non-voters do; past voting predicts better; and multi-item likely-voter indices beat single 'certain to vote' items.
findings.quant: Rogers and Aida (American Politics Research, online 5 Sept 2013, DOI 10.1177/1532673X13496453): seven pre-election surveys with post-election validation across three US elections, N=29,403. Both 'flake-out' (self-predicted voters who abstain) and 'flake-in' (self-predicted non-voters who vote) are common; vote history (file or recall) predicts turnout better than self-prediction; self-predicted voters and non-voters barely differ demographically, although actual voters do. Pew Research Center (18 May 2001; Dimock, AAPOR 2001): 1999 Philadelphia mayoral race, 2,415 registered voters in two waves matched to voting records. An eight-item likely-voter index classified 73% correctly (17% screened out but voted, 10% screened in but did not); single items such as 'plan to vote' classify too many people as likely voters; the likely-voter estimate matched actual voters better than registered voters (a 3-point Street lead vs a dead heat). Morin-Chasse, Bol, Stephenson and Labbe St-Vincent (PSRM 5(3): 575-584, 2017, DOI 10.1017/psrm.2016.31): face-saving response options cut turnout over-reporting by 0 to 18 points across 19 post-election surveys in Europe and Canada.

findings.claim: Recall-based items are unreliable in the 2026 campaign. JPPI shows respondents' recalled 'before the war' self-placement matches past direct measurement, while their 'today' placement overstates the move to the strong right by about 10 points against a direct same-year measurement. Vote-flow tables built on recalled 2022 vote need the same caution.

Direct nine-point measurement without reference to the war: July 2025 13%, July 2026 14%. 33% report shifting right, 14% left, 54% no change. JPPI suggests the discrepancy may come from wording that invites respondents to report a change.

challenges.title: Do not add a bloc-turnout term from self-reported intention, or add it only as a heavily shrunk differential
challenges.what_literature_says: 2026 polls consistently show opposition voters 5-7 points more certain to vote (PBV-F07). challenges.current_model: No bloc-differential turnout term. CHURN_SPLIT gives change-bloc movers a higher abstention share (0.172 vs 0.079), from the 2021-22 kalpi matrix.
challenges.proposed_change: If a term is wanted: bloc turnout differential ~ Normal(mu, sd) with mu = 0.2 x the polled intention gap (about +1 point of turnout toward the change bloc) and sd equal to mu, applied to the Jewish blocs only.
